title: Outcome Bias
hook: A lucky sellout can make a sloppy choice look like genius.
coreIdea: Outcome bias judges a decision by the result alone, letting good results flatter bad process and bad results stain sound process.
counterintuition: Outcomes matter, but they are not the whole verdict. A useful review asks whether the process was sound before the result started telling its story.
tryThisNow: Pick one finished decision and cover the result. Rate the process from the evidence, options, risks, and reasoning that existed beforehand.
keyTakeaway: Grade the decision process before the outcome gets a vote.

breakdown.fastRead:
A health permit sleeve sits beside the restaurant menu test after the new dish sells out in one night. Charlotte's team wants to declare the test brilliant. The result is good. The process may still be thin.

Outcome bias lets the result grade the decision. If the dish sells, the test looks smart. If it fails, the same test looks foolish. Either way, the outcome can drown out the question that matters: was the decision made well from what was known then?

A win can still come from a bad bet.

The correction is to inspect process quality: evidence used, alternatives considered, risks named, and decision record kept before the result arrived.
breakdown.deepRead:
The health permit sleeve in Charlotte's kitchen holds the launch checklist for the new menu item. The dish sold out, but the team never checked prep time under a full Saturday load, allergen questions, or whether the high-margin side crowded out another dish. Charlotte writes outcome bias on the sleeve and asks for the decision record before expanding the item.

A result is information. It should not be ignored. The sellout teaches something about demand. But it does not prove the test was well designed. A lucky result can reward a careless process, just as an unlucky result can punish a careful process. If you only judge from the finish line, you train the team to worship luck.

Results teach more when process is visible.

A process review asks what was knowable before the outcome. Did the team define success? Did it list risks? Did it compare options? Did it decide what evidence would change the plan? If those pieces were missing, the sellout is useful news, not proof of good judgment.

A legal-aid triage desk makes the point in a more serious setting. Ivan holds a shelf scan of case files after a rejected case unexpectedly wins on appeal. Staff now want to say the triage was wrong. Ivan marks process quality on the scan and rereads the notes that existed before the new evidence appeared.

A good outcome can expose new facts without proving the old decision was bad.
breakdown.fullRead:
A museum gallery smells of fresh paint and waxed floorboards while Marit opens the exhibit checklist beside a donor report. The donor-backed exhibit drew record attendance. The board wants to praise the approval process and repeat it. Marit sees a problem: the vote happened before conservation costs, crowd flow, and education staffing were fully checked.

Outcome bias is powerful because results feel final. A full gallery, a winning lawsuit, a profitable trade, a healed patient, a successful launch: the result arrives with authority. Once it arrives, the process starts to look better or worse in its light. The mind asks whether it worked, then quietly treats that as the same question as whether the decision was good.

Jonathan Baron and John Hershey studied this pattern in decision evaluation: people judged the quality of a decision differently when they knew the outcome, even when the decision process itself was the same. That matters because a decision can be good under uncertainty and still lose. It can also be poor and get rescued by luck.

What would you think of this decision if the result were still unknown?

Marit uses that question on the museum record. The exhibit's attendance goes in one column. The decision process goes in another: evidence reviewed, risks named, missing checks, dissent recorded, and alternatives considered. The attendance result says the exhibit attracted visitors. It does not erase the process gaps. The next donor exhibit gets a stronger checklist, not a blank endorsement of the old approval.

You can feel the same pull in a hardware storm inventory review. You are looking at a training frame from a staff video after Aaron overstocked generators before a storm. The storm hit, the generators sold, and everyone calls him sharp. Aaron marks known information on the frame and asks whether the forecast, supplier terms, and unsold-stock risk justified the order before the storm proved him lucky.

This is not a plea to ignore outcomes. Outcomes close the feedback loop.

The danger is resulting: letting the outcome replace the review. A bad result may reveal a process flaw, but it may also reveal bad luck inside a sound process. A good result may reveal a smart bet, but it may also reveal luck inside a weak process. The only way to know is to preserve the decision record.

So separate the two grades. Grade the process from the evidence available before the outcome. Then grade the result as new information. When those grades disagree, pay attention. That disagreement is where the learning lives.

Grade the decision process before the outcome gets a vote.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Outcome bias rewards and punishes decisions for results they did not fully control. Readers need to separate process quality from outcome quality before learning the wrong lesson.

reviewCards.front: A decision turns out well. What should you check before praising it?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the process used good evidence, alternatives, risk review, and a clear decision record before the outcome arrived.

reviewCards.front: Why can a bad result mislead a postmortem?
reviewCards.back: It can make a sound process look foolish because the result is emotionally loud.
It is judging the quality of a decision mainly by the result instead of the process that produced it.

reviewCards.front: How do you review a lucky win?
reviewCards.back: Keep the win as feedback, but ask whether the pre-outcome process deserves to be repeated.

reviewCards.front: What record protects against outcome bias?
reviewCards.back: A decision record with known information, options, risks, assumptions, dissent, and success criteria.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to grade process quality before letting outcome quality shape the verdict.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a decision has a loud result, then I will review the decision record before praising or blaming the process.
If a test fails, then I will separate test design quality from the result before discarding the idea.
If a risky choice succeeds, then I will ask whether the process would still deserve repeating if the result had gone badly.
If I regret an outcome, then I will reconstruct the evidence and options I had before judging the original choice.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one finished decision and write two grades: process quality and outcome quality. Do not let one erase the other.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, create a short decision record before acting: known information, options, risks, and what would count as success.
